rewritten_text:
We grew up together, less than a year apart in age. I hardly need say that we knew no quarrels or estrangement. Harmony lay at the heart of our companionship, and the differences and contrasts between our personalities brought us closer. Elizabeth was calmer and more self-contained, but despite my passionate nature, I could concentrate more intensely and felt a deeper thirst for knowledge. She occupied herself with the poets’ flights of imagination. In the majestic, extraordinary landscapes surrounding our Swiss home—the sublime mountain forms, the changing seasons, storms and stillness, winter’s silence, and the life and tumult of our Alpine summers—she found endless reasons for wonder and delight. While my companion contemplated the magnificent appearance of things with solemn contentment, I took pleasure in investigating their causes. To me, the world was a secret I wanted to uncover. Curiosity, an earnest search for nature’s hidden laws, and joy approaching ecstasy as those laws revealed themselves are among the earliest feelings I remember.

When their second son was born, seven years younger than me, my parents abandoned their traveling life altogether and settled in their native country. We owned a house in Geneva and a country home at Belrive, on the lake’s eastern shore, a little more than three miles from the city. We lived mainly at the latter, where my parents led fairly secluded lives. I naturally avoided crowds and formed passionate attachments to a few people. Consequently, most of my schoolmates meant little to me, but with one I developed the closest possible friendship. Henry Clerval was the son of a Geneva merchant, a boy of remarkable talent and imagination. He loved bold undertakings, hardship, and even danger for its own sake. He read widely in tales of chivalry and romance. He composed heroic songs and began writing numerous stories of enchantment and knightly adventure. He tried to persuade us to perform plays and take part in masquerades, taking our characters from the heroes of Roncesvalles, King Arthur’s Round Table, and the companies of knights who shed their blood to reclaim the Holy Sepulchre from those they called unbelievers.

No one could have had a happier childhood than I did. My parents embodied kindness and indulgence. We never saw them as tyrants directing our lives according to their whims. Instead, we understood that they were the people who created and provided all the many pleasures we enjoyed.

But how could I, a poor, bewildered village boy, escape the remarkable inconsistency that catches even the best and wisest people every day?

“That may all be true,” I told Biddy, “but I admire her terribly.”

At that, I rolled onto my face, seized the hair on both sides of my head, and pulled it hard. All the while, I knew my heart was so foolish and so badly mistaken that I felt my face would have deserved it if I had lifted my head by the hair and banged it against the pebbles, as punishment for belonging to such an idiot.

Biddy was the wisest of girls and stopped trying to reason with me. Her hand, though rough from work, was comforting. She laid it over each of mine in turn and gently released them from my hair. Then she softly patted my shoulder to soothe me while I cried a little into my sleeve, exactly as I had in the brewery yard. I had a vague conviction that somebody—or perhaps everybody—was treating me very badly. I couldn’t have said which.

“I’m glad of one thing,” Biddy said. “You felt you could trust me with this, Pip. And I’m glad of something else: you know, of course, that I’ll keep your secret and always deserve your trust that far. If your first teacher—oh dear, such a poor teacher, with so much to learn herself!—were still teaching you now, she thinks she knows what lesson she would give you. But it would be a difficult one to learn, and you’ve moved beyond her, so there’s no use in it now.” With a quiet sigh for me, Biddy stood up from the bank. Then, brightening her voice, she said, “Shall we walk a little farther or go home?”

“Biddy,” I cried, rising, putting my arm around her neck, and kissing her, “I’ll always tell you everything.”

“Until you’re a gentleman,” said Biddy.

“You know I’ll never be one, so that means always. Not that I need to tell you anything—you already know everything I know, as I told you at home the other night.”

“Ah!” Biddy said, almost in a whisper, looking away toward the ships. Then she repeated, in the same pleasant, brighter voice, “Shall we walk a little farther or go home?”

I told Biddy we would walk a little farther, and we did. The summer afternoon softened into a summer evening, and it was very beautiful.

Two years passed in this way. Hundreds of days followed one another. They brought no outward changes, but a few slow changes took place in my mind as I drifted toward death. I began to study more and to connect more deeply with other people’s thoughts as I found them in books. I read history and lost my sense of myself among the crowds who had lived before me. Perhaps, as the first sharp pain of suffering faded, I became more human. Solitude, too, lost some of its appeal. I began to want understanding again. I was never tempted to join a crowd, but I wished for one friend who would love me. Perhaps you will say that I was gradually becoming ready to return to society. I do not think so. The understanding I wanted had to be so pure, so free of outside influences, that the coarse concerns always mixed into even the world’s best feelings would certainly have disappointed me. Believe me, I was less prepared then for contact with other people than I had been before. When I left them, they had tormented me as pain or illness might: something outside my mind irritated it, and I wanted to cast it off. Now, however, I would have longed for understanding. I would have wanted to bind my soul to someone else’s, and so would have prepared abundant disappointment and suffering for myself. I was as delicate as the sensitive plant, all exposed nerves. I did not want encouragement or help in pursuing ambition or knowledge. I wanted sweet, shared affection, smiles to lift my spirits, and gentle words of comfort. I wished for one heart into which I could pour my complaints freely, hoping its heavenly goodness might make blessed fruit grow from such bitter seeds. But how could I find this? The love at the heart of friendship is a gentle spirit, rarely found unless two kind people have been close since childhood or are joined by shared suffering and interests. For a chosen few, it arrives unexpectedly and without being sought. It falls like soft dew on favored places, making even previously barren ground fertile with every sweet plant. But when pursued, it flees. It mocks the prayers of those who worship it. It offers itself, but refuses to be hunted.

I knew all this and did not go looking for understanding. Yet there on my lonely heath, beneath my humble roof, with emptiness all around, it came to me like a winter sunbeam, brightening the drifted snow while helping it melt. Alas, that sun shone on ruined fruit. I did not recover beneath its light, for I was too completely broken to feel its healing warmth.
